question: Which two majestic divine titles are paired in Psalm 91:1 to emphasize God's supreme transcendence and all-sufficient protection?
opt1: The most High (Elyon) and the Almighty (Shaddai)
opt2: The LORD of hosts (Yahweh Sabaoth) and the Everlasting Father (El Olam)
opt3: The Creator (Boreh) and the King of glory (Melek HaKavod)
opt4: The God of Jacob (Elohei Yaakov) and the Holy One of Israel (Kadosh Yisrael)
correct: The most High (Elyon) and the Almighty (Shaddai)
explanation: The psalm opens pairing two exalted divine titles: Elyon ('most High') emphasizing sovereign supremacy, and Shaddai ('the Almighty') conveying invincible power and sheltering sufficiency. Psalm 91:1 (KJV) - "He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty."

question: What fourfold personal confession of faith does the psalmist declare concerning the LORD in Psalm 91:2?
opt1: He is my shepherd, my king, my redeemer, and my horn of salvation
opt2: He is my refuge, my fortress, my God, and in Him will I trust
opt3: He is my light, my shield, my buckler, and my rock of defence
opt4: He is my deliverer, my high tower, my hiding place, and my song
correct: He is my refuge, my fortress, my God, and in Him will I trust
explanation: The psalmist appropriates God through four personal affirmations of absolute covenant security: refuge, fortress, God, and the object of total trust. Psalm 91:2 (KJV) - "I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust."

question: From which two perilous dangers does Psalm 91:3 guarantee divine deliverance for the believer?
opt1: The sword of the enemy and the pit of destruction
opt2: The wrath of kings and the flood of great waters
opt3: The snare of the fowler and the noisome pestilence
opt4: The venom of asps and the drought of the wilderness
correct: The snare of the fowler and the noisome pestilence
explanation: God delivers from both hidden spiritual/human entrapments ('the snare of the fowler') and contagious, destructive plagues ('the noisome pestilence'). Psalm 91:3 (KJV) - "Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence."

question: What comforting avian imagery is used in Psalm 91:4 to portray God's tender protective care over His people?
opt1: He shall bear thee on eagle wings, and hide thee in the clefts of the rocks
opt2: He shall nest thee in celestial branches, and shelter thee from storms
opt3: He shall hover as a mother dove, and brood over thy tabernacle
opt4: He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust
correct: He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust
explanation: The psalmist uses maternal bird imagery to illustrate affectionate and impenetrable divine protection, backed by the solid defensive armor of divine truth. Psalm 91:4 (KJV) - "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler."

question: Which four dread perils spanning day and night are believers shielded from according to Psalm 91:5-6?
opt1: Terror by night, arrow that flieth by day, pestilence that walketh in darkness, and destruction that wasteth at noonday
opt2: Robbers in the night, spears at noon, pestilence in the evening, and burning heat at midday
opt3: Nightmares of the soul, daytime ambush, creeping shadows, and famine at harvest
opt4: Snares of darkness, arrows of the wicked, diseases of dawn, and storms of twilight
correct: Terror by night, arrow that flieth by day, pestilence that walketh in darkness, and destruction that wasteth at noonday
explanation: God provides comprehensive, round-the-clock immunity covering every terrifying threat whether nocturnal or diurnal, visible or covert. Psalm 91:5-6 (KJV) - "Thou shalt not be afraid for the terror by night; nor for the arrow that flieth by day; Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness; nor for the destruction that wasteth at noonday."

question: What dramatic contrast in casualties does Psalm 91:7 highlight between surrounding destruction and the sheltered believer?
opt1: A hundred shall flee at thy presence, and a thousand at thy shout, yet thou shalt stand untouched
opt2: A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand, but it shall not come nigh thee
opt3: Thousands shall perish in the siege, and myriad armies be slain, yet thy house shall be preserved
opt4: Seven times shall the wicked stumble, and seventy times fall, but thou shalt walk in safety
correct: A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand, but it shall not come nigh thee
explanation: Even amidst catastrophic, widespread fatalities falling in thousands and tens of thousands, divine protection creates an invulnerable perimeter around the faithful. Psalm 91:7 (KJV) - "A thousand shall fall at thy side, and ten thousand at thy right hand; but it shall not come nigh thee."

question: Which verses from Psalm 91 did Satan quote to Jesus Christ during the wilderness temptation in Matthew 4:6 and Luke 4:10-11?
opt1: Psalm 91:1-2, concerning dwelling under the shadow of the Almighty
opt2: Psalm 91:5-6, concerning not fearing the terror by night nor arrows by day
opt3: Psalm 91:11-12, concerning angels bearing Him up lest He dash His foot against a stone
opt4: Psalm 91:13-14, concerning treading upon the lion and adder
correct: Psalm 91:11-12, concerning angels bearing Him up lest He dash His foot against a stone
explanation: Satan subtly quoted Psalm 91:11-12 to tempt Christ into presumption, maliciously omitting 'to keep thee in all thy ways' to test God rather than trust Him. Psalm 91:11-12 (KJV) - "For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. They shall bear thee up in their hands, lest thou dash thy foot against a stone."

question: Which dangerous predators and venomous creatures are believers promised power to trample under feet in Psalm 91:13?
opt1: The wolf and viper, the leopard and the scorpion
opt2: The bear and cockatrice, the basilisk and the serpent
opt3: The wild boar and asp, the hyena and the leviathan
opt4: The lion and adder, the young lion and the dragon
correct: The lion and adder, the young lion and the dragon
explanation: Believers are granted triumphant dominion over fierce open adversaries ('the lion') and subtle venomous foes ('adder' and 'dragon'), prefiguring Christ's words in Luke 10:19. Psalm 91:13 (KJV) - "Thou shalt tread upon the lion and adder: the young lion and the dragon shalt thou trample under feet."

question: What two conditions on the part of the believer prompt God's direct oracle of deliverance and exaltation in Psalm 91:14?
opt1: Setting his love upon the LORD, and knowing His name
opt2: Offering burnt sacrifices daily, and fasting before the sanctuary
opt3: Keeping all ceremonial ordinances, and giving tithes of all possessions
opt4: Smiting the heathen nations, and establishing David's dynasty
correct: Setting his love upon the LORD, and knowing His name
explanation: God Himself speaks in the first person, promising deliverance and elevation because of relational affection ('set his love upon me') and spiritual intimacy ('known my name'). Psalm 91:14 (KJV) - "Because he hath set his love upon me, therefore will I deliver him: I will set him on high, because he hath known my name."

question: With which two ultimate blessings does the Lord conclude His divine oracle in Psalm 91:16?
opt1: Crowning him with earthly wealth, and giving him victory over all kings
opt2: Satisfying him with long life, and showing him His salvation
opt3: Building him an enduring dynasty, and filling his storehouses with grain
opt4: Seating him among the princes, and giving him peace in old age
correct: Satisfying him with long life, and showing him His salvation
explanation: The climax of God's covenant pledge encompasses both temporal abundance ('long life') and eternal spiritual beatitude ('my salvation'). Psalm 91:16 (KJV) - "With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation."

question: What unique liturgical designation appears in the superscription of Psalm 92, found nowhere else in the entire Psalter?
opt1: 'A Psalm or Song for the day of atonement'
opt2: 'A Psalm or Song for the sabbath day'
opt3: 'A Psalm or Song for the feast of tabernacles'
opt4: 'A Psalm or Song for the morning sacrifice'
correct: 'A Psalm or Song for the sabbath day'
explanation: Psalm 92 is the sole psalm in the Hebrew canon explicitly assigned by its title for use on the weekly Sabbath day. Psalm 92:Title (KJV) - "A Psalm or Song for the sabbath day."

question: According to Psalm 92:1-2, what daily twofold rhythm of praise is declared to be 'a good thing'?
opt1: To offer morning incense at sunrise, and evening prayers at twilight
opt2: To meditate on the law at dawn, and confess transgressions at midnight
opt3: To show forth God's lovingkindness in the morning, and His faithfulness every night
opt4: To sing songs of Zion at daybreak, and fast before sleep
correct: To show forth God's lovingkindness in the morning, and His faithfulness every night
explanation: True sabbath worship encompasses bookending each day with God's steadfast love (chesed) at sunrise and His unwavering reliability (emunah) at nightfall. Psalm 92:1-2 (KJV) - "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD, and to sing praises unto thy name, O most High: To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night,"

question: Which musical instruments are specified in Psalm 92:3 to accompany this sabbath celebration?
opt1: The cornet, the flute, and the high-sounding cymbals
opt2: The trumpet of rams' horn, the timbrel, and the pipe
opt3: The sackbut, the dulcimer, and strings of silver
opt4: An instrument of ten strings, the psaltery, and the harp with a solemn sound
correct: An instrument of ten strings, the psaltery, and the harp with a solemn sound
explanation: Praise is enriched by a full Levitical string consort: the ten-stringed decachord, the psaltery (harp/lute), and the kinnor with meditative solemnity (higgaion). Psalm 92:3 (KJV) - "Upon an instrument of ten strings, and upon the psaltery; upon the harp with a solemn sound."

question: How does Psalm 92:6 describe those who fail to perceive the majesty of God's works and the depth of His thoughts?
opt1: A brutish man knoweth not, neither doth a fool understand this
opt2: A wicked man hateth it, and the hypocrite closeth his eyes
opt3: The heathen mock at it, and the simple are led astray
opt4: The scorner blasphemeth, and the proud regardeth it not
correct: A brutish man knoweth not, neither doth a fool understand this
explanation: Spiritual dullness and lack of perception belong to animalistic ('brutish') instincts and moral folly, blind to God's profound works and deep thoughts. Psalm 92:5-6 (KJV) - "O LORD, how great are thy works! and thy thoughts are very deep. A brutish man knoweth not; neither doth a fool understand this."

question: To what fast-growing yet ephemeral vegetation does Psalm 92:7 compare the temporary flourishing of the wicked?
opt1: They flourish as mushrooms that wither in the morning sun
opt2: They spring as the grass, only that they shall be destroyed for ever
opt3: They blossom like weeds that choke the wheat and are burned
opt4: They shoot forth as vines that yield wild and bitter grapes
correct: They spring as the grass, only that they shall be destroyed for ever
explanation: The flourishing of evil workers is not enduring prosperity, but rather rapid growth akin to common grass, ripening them for eternal judgment. Psalm 92:7 (KJV) - "When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; it is that they shall be destroyed for ever:"

question: In contrast to the doomed flourishing of the wicked in verse 7, what is declared of the LORD in Psalm 92:8?
opt1: The LORD shall break them with a rod of iron
opt2: God sitteth upon the circle of the earth
opt3: Thou, LORD, art most high for evermore
opt4: The Lord of hosts shall judge all flesh in righteousness
correct: Thou, LORD, art most high for evermore
explanation: Placed at the structural center of the psalm, verse 8 proclaims Yahweh's immutable and eternal sovereignty, standing exalted forever above transience. Psalm 92:8 (KJV) - "But thou, LORD, art most high for evermore."

question: What two vivid metaphors of vigor and divine favor does the psalmist claim in Psalm 92:10?
opt1: His feet made like hinds' feet, and his head crowned with gold
opt2: His strength renewed like the eagle, and his hands bathed in milk
opt3: His bow made strong in battle, and his lips sweetened with honey
opt4: His horn exalted like the horn of an unicorn, and being anointed with fresh oil
correct: His horn exalted like the horn of an unicorn, and being anointed with fresh oil
explanation: The horn of the wild ox ('unicorn') represents majestic, invincible vigor, while 'fresh green oil' signifies renewed spiritual consecration and joy. Psalm 92:10 (KJV) - "But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: I shall be anointed with fresh oil."

question: To which two majestic trees are the righteous compared in Psalm 92:12 to illustrate their flourishing vitality?
opt1: Flourishing like the palm tree, and growing like a cedar in Lebanon
opt2: Fruitful like the olive tree, and spread out like the green bay tree
opt3: Upright like the cypress, and rooted like the oak of Bashan
opt4: Sweet like the fig tree, and blossoming like the almond rod
correct: Flourishing like the palm tree, and growing like a cedar in Lebanon
explanation: The righteous possess the upright, fruitful grace of the date palm and the enduring, incorruptible strength of the Lebanese cedar. Psalm 92:12 (KJV) - "The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon."

question: What extraordinary blessing is promised in Psalm 92:14 to those planted in the house of the LORD?
opt1: Their eyes shall not dim, nor their natural force be abated
opt2: They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing
opt3: They shall see their children's children unto the fourth generation
opt4: They shall be preserved from all sickness, and die without pain
correct: They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing
explanation: Defying physical decline, those deeply rooted in God's presence maintain perpetual spiritual vitality, bearing ripe fruit into their final years. Psalm 92:14 (KJV) - "They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing;"

question: What ultimate theological truth does the lifelong flourishing of the righteous demonstrate according to Psalm 92:15?
opt1: To prove that the seed of Abraham shall inherit the earth
opt2: To manifest that keeping the ceremonial law brings long life
opt3: To show that the LORD is upright: He is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in Him
opt4: To confirm that wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness
correct: To show that the LORD is upright: He is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in Him
explanation: The preservation and fruitful old age of the godly serve as living testimonies to God's spotless righteousness, fidelity, and unshakeable rock-like stability. Psalm 92:15 (KJV) - "To shew that the LORD is upright: he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him."

question: With which two glorious royal garments is the LORD described as clothed and girded in Psalm 93:1?
opt1: He is clothed with light as with a garment, and girded with truth
opt2: He is clothed with righteousness, and girded with vengeance
opt3: He is clothed with majesty, and clothed with strength wherewith He hath girded Himself
opt4: He is clothed with salvation, and girded with glorious power
correct: He is clothed with majesty, and clothed with strength wherewith He hath girded Himself
explanation: As absolute Sovereign, Yahweh's regal robes are majesty and His warrior belt is divine omnipotent strength. Psalm 93:1 (KJV) - "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the LORD is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself: the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved."

question: What foundational effect does the sovereign reign of the LORD produce upon the physical creation in Psalm 93:1?
opt1: The foundations of the hills melt like wax before Him
opt2: The pillars of the earth tremble and shake at His voice
opt3: The heavens drop dew and the clouds rain down righteousness
opt4: The world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved
correct: The world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved
explanation: Because God reigns supreme, the moral and cosmological order of the world is fixed and secure, anchored against chaotic dissolution. Psalm 93:1 (KJV) - "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the LORD is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself: the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved."

question: How does Psalm 93:2 articulate the eternal, pre-temporal existence of God and His royal throne?
opt1: Thy throne is established of old: thou art from everlasting
opt2: Thy throne is set in the third heaven: thy dominion endureth for generations
opt3: Thy kingdom was prepared from the foundation of the world: thou art eternal
opt4: Thy sceptre is righteous from antiquity: thou art the Alpha and Omega
correct: Thy throne is established of old: thou art from everlasting
explanation: God's kingship did not begin at creation; His throne is established from eternity past ('of old'), and He Himself is 'from everlasting'. Psalm 93:2 (KJV) - "Thy throne is established of old: thou art from everlasting."

question: What threefold poetic repetition in Psalm 93:3 portrays the surging threat of chaotic and rebellious forces?
opt1: The heathen rage, the kings take counsel, the rulers set themselves against the LORD
opt2: The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their waves
opt3: The seas roar, the depths tremble, the billows break against the shore
opt4: The winds blow, the storm ariseth, the tempest beateth upon the sanctuary
correct: The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their waves
explanation: A master example of climactic parallelism where 'the floods' lift up first their presence, then their voice, and finally their crashing waves. Psalm 93:3 (KJV) - "The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their waves."

question: How does Psalm 93:4 contrast the supremacy of the LORD with the roaring power of the raging seas?
opt1: The LORD rebukeeth the red sea, and drieth up the fountains of the deep
opt2: The voice of the LORD stilleth the tempest, and maketh the storm a calm
opt3: The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea
opt4: The Lord of hosts treadeth upon the high places of the sea with His chariots
correct: The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea
explanation: No tumult of primeval waters or raging nations can challenge the transcendent majesty of Yahweh enthroned on high. Psalm 93:4 (KJV) - "The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea."

question: Which two enduring qualities are affirmed of God's revelation and His sanctuary in Psalm 93:5?
opt1: Thy commandments are pure: glory filleth thy temple without end
opt2: Thy covenants are unchangeable: praise waiteth for thee in Zion eternally
opt3: Thy judgments are righteous: mercy compasseth thy dwelling place
opt4: Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, O LORD, for ever
correct: Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, O LORD, for ever
explanation: The psalm culminates in the unshakable certainty of God's written word ('testimonies') and the eternal moral sanctity of His dwelling ('holiness'). Psalm 93:5 (KJV) - "Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, O LORD, for ever."

question: Into which distinctive canonical group of psalms celebrating the universal kingship of God does Psalm 93 serve as the opening anthem?
opt1: The Enthronement Psalms (Psalms 93, 95-99)
opt2: The Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120-134)
opt3: The Penitential Psalms (Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143)
opt4: The Egyptian Hallel (Psalms 113-118)
correct: The Enthronement Psalms (Psalms 93, 95-99)
explanation: Psalm 93 inaugurates the majestic collection of theocratic Enthronement Psalms proclaiming 'Yahweh Malak' (The LORD reigneth). Psalm 93:1 (KJV) - "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty; the LORD is clothed with strength, wherewith he hath girded himself: the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved."

question: In Hebrew poetry and biblical theology, what do the turbulent 'floods' and 'many waters' of Psalm 93:3-4 primarily symbolize?
opt1: The abundant seasonal rains sent to water the Promised Land
opt2: The chaotic forces of cosmic chaos and the rebellious, threatening pagan nations
opt3: The tears of penitent believers shed during national fasts
opt4: The cleansing waters of ceremonial Levitical washings
correct: The chaotic forces of cosmic chaos and the rebellious, threatening pagan nations
explanation: In biblical symbolism, the raging floods represent both metaphysical chaos and hostile geopolitical empires rising against God's kingdom. Psalm 93:3-4 (KJV) - "The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their waves. The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea."

question: Why does Psalm 93 connect the stability of the physical world in verse 1 with God's established throne in verse 2?
opt1: To argue that the earth is physically suspended upon literal immovable pillars
opt2: To teach that political empires will never fall from world history
opt3: To show that cosmological order and physical stability depend entirely upon God's eternal sovereign governance
opt4: To prove that natural disasters are completely impossible under divine rule
correct: To show that cosmological order and physical stability depend entirely upon God's eternal sovereign governance
explanation: The stability of creation is rooted not in autonomous physical laws, but in the eternal, pre-existing throne and sovereign will of the Creator. Psalm 93:1-2 (KJV) - "The LORD reigneth, he is clothed with majesty ... the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved. Thy throne is established of old: thou art from everlasting."

question: What is meant by the phrase 'holiness becometh thine house, O LORD, for ever' in Psalm 93:5?
opt1: Holiness will only be required of the temple during the millennial reign
opt2: The house of God is made holy exclusively by the amount of gold within it
opt3: Priestly rituals supersede moral righteousness in the presence of God
opt4: Holiness is the perpetual, fitting, and beautiful adornment of God's sanctuary
correct: Holiness is the perpetual, fitting, and beautiful adornment of God's sanctuary
explanation: 'Becometh' (Hebrew: na'awah) denotes that which is proper, lovely, and fitting; moral sanctity is the indispensable adornment of God's presence. Psalm 93:5 (KJV) - "Thy testimonies are very sure: holiness becometh thine house, O LORD, for ever."

question: What title does the psalmist twice ascribe to God in Psalm 94:1 when invoking Him to intervene against rampant wickedness?
opt1: 'O God, who delightest in mercy'
opt2: 'O Lord of hosts, who art slow to anger'
opt3: 'O Judge, who keepest covenant forever'
opt4: 'O God, to whom vengeance belongeth'
correct: 'O God, to whom vengeance belongeth'
explanation: Vengeance belongs exclusively to God (Deuteronomy 32:35, Romans 12:19); therefore the psalmist appeals to the sovereign Judge to shine forth in judicial rectitude. Psalm 94:1 (KJV) - "O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongeth; O God, to whom vengeance belongeth, shew thyself."

question: Which three vulnerable groups, protected under divine covenant law, are murdered by the wicked according to Psalm 94:6?
opt1: The widow, the stranger, and the fatherless
opt2: The poor, the needy, and the debtor
opt3: The Levite, the captive, and the sick
opt4: The infant, the aged, and the bondservant
correct: The widow, the stranger, and the fatherless
explanation: The ultimate depths of tyranny are revealed when oppressors prey upon the classic biblical triad of helpless dependents: widows, strangers, and orphans. Psalm 94:6 (KJV) - "They slay the widow and the stranger, and murder the fatherless."

question: What practical atheism and blindness do the wicked express concerning God's awareness in Psalm 94:7?
opt1: There is no God in heaven to judge the sons of men
opt2: The LORD shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it
opt3: God is too far removed in the clouds to care for Israel
opt4: Our own right hand hath gotten us the victory, not God
correct: The LORD shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it
explanation: The oppressors deceive themselves into believing that the covenant God of Israel is oblivious and indifferent to their blatant atrocities. Psalm 94:7 (KJV) - "Yet they say, The LORD shall not see, neither shall the God of Jacob regard it."

question: What brilliant epistemological argument from intelligent design does Psalm 94:9 use to refute those who think God is oblivious?
opt1: He that made the tongue, shall He not speak? He that formed the brain, shall He not know?
opt2: He that gave the breath of life, shall He not judge? He that weighed the dust, shall He not see?
opt3: He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see?
opt4: He that commanded the light, shall He not discern? He that created the heart, shall He not understand?
correct: He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see?
explanation: The Designer of sensory faculties must infinitely possess the very faculties He created; the Architect of human hearing and vision cannot be deaf or blind. Psalm 94:9 (KJV) - "He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? he that formed the eye, shall he not see?"

question: What verdict does Psalm 94:11 deliver on the vain thoughts of mankind, later quoted by the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:20?
opt1: The imaginations of man are evil from his youth continually
opt2: All the wisdom of this world is foolishness before God
opt3: Man in his best state is altogether a breath and a shadow
opt4: The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity
correct: The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity
explanation: God penetrates the inward mental counsels of fallen human reasoning, discerning that in themselves they are utter futility and vanity. Psalm 94:11 (KJV) - "The LORD knoweth the thoughts of man, that they are vanity."

question: According to Psalm 94:12, who is pronounced 'blessed'?
opt1: Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD, and teachest him out of thy law
opt2: Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly
opt3: Blessed is the man unto whom the LORD imputeth not iniquity
opt4: Blessed are they that dwell in thy house, praising thee continually
correct: Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD, and teachest him out of thy law
explanation: True spiritual beatitude combines loving divine discipline (musar) with scriptural instruction from God's holy law (torah). Psalm 94:12 (KJV) - "Blessed is the man whom thou chastenest, O LORD, and teachest him out of thy law;"

question: What unconditional covenant pledge does Psalm 94:14 make concerning Israel, reaffirmed by Paul in Romans 11:1-2?
opt1: The house of Jacob shall be an everlasting flame among the nations
opt2: The LORD will not cast off his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance
opt3: The seed of David shall endure as the days of heaven forever
opt4: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah until Shiloh come
correct: The LORD will not cast off his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance
explanation: Despite national chastening and foreign oppression, God's election of His covenant inheritance remains irrevocable. Psalm 94:14 (KJV) - "For the LORD will not cast off his people, neither will he forsake his inheritance."

question: In Psalm 94:18-19, what two divine actions brought support and delight to the psalmist's anxious heart?
opt1: When enemies attacked, God's shield defended him; in dark nights, His light shone upon him
opt2: When he stumbled, angels carried him; in sorrow, holy wine cheered his countenance
opt3: When his foot slipped, God's mercy held him up; in a multitude of thoughts, God's comforts delighted his soul
opt4: When sickness struck, God's hand healed him; in loneliness, His voice brought peace
correct: When his foot slipped, God's mercy held him up; in a multitude of thoughts, God's comforts delighted his soul
explanation: Covenant steadfast love (chesed) prevents the believer from falling, and intimate divine consolations bring profound joy amidst overwhelming anxious thoughts. Psalm 94:18-19 (KJV) - "When I said, My foot slippeth; thy mercy, O LORD, held me up. In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul."

question: How does Psalm 94:20 denounce corrupt rulers who legalize wickedness?
opt1: Shall unjust judges sit in Moses' seat, who pervert judgment for bribes?
opt2: Can a corrupt king stand before the holy God, who decrees evil decrees?
opt3: Shall the council of ungodly rulers reign with Christ, who oppress the righteous?
opt4: Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
correct: Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
explanation: God rejects any alliance with oppressive judicial systems or state authorities that institutionalize injustice under the color of legal statutes. Psalm 94:20 (KJV) - "Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?"

question: How does Psalm 94 conclude in verse 23 regarding the ultimate destiny of corrupt persecutors?
opt1: He shall bring upon them their own iniquity, and shall cut them off in their own wickedness
opt2: He shall deliver them to the sword of Babylon, and their houses to fire
opt3: He shall scatter them into the four winds, and blot out their name under heaven
opt4: He shall condemn them to outer darkness, where is weeping and gnashing of teeth
correct: He shall bring upon them their own iniquity, and shall cut them off in their own wickedness
explanation: In divine retributive justice, the very evil the wicked devised rebounds upon them, resulting in total and final cut-off by the LORD. Psalm 94:23 (KJV) - "And he shall bring upon them their own iniquity, and shall cut them off in their own wickedness; yea, the LORD our God shall cut them off."

question: What traditional Latin title is given to Psalm 95 due to its opening liturgical invitation in verse 1 ('O come')?
opt1: The Venite

opt4: The Benedictus
correct: The Venite

question: How is the supremacy of Yahweh proclaimed over all rival entities in Psalm 95:3?
opt1: For our God is in the heavens, and doth whatsoever pleaseth Him
opt2: For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods
opt3: For the gods of the nations are silver and gold, but the LORD is eternal
opt4: For He is high above the nations, and His glory above the heavens
correct: For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods
explanation: Yahweh's majesty is affirmed as sovereign Emperor ('great King') exalted far above any supposed angelic or pagan deities. Psalm 95:3 (KJV) - "For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods."

question: Which geological and geographic realms are described as belonging to God's hand and workmanship in Psalm 95:4-5?
opt1: The highest heavens, the clouds of the sky, the rivers, and the valleys
opt2: The foundations of Zion, the wilderness of Sinai, the Jordan river, and Lebanon
opt3: The deep places of the earth, the strength of the hills, the sea, and the dry land
opt4: The stars in their courses, the sun at noonday, the oceans, and the fertile plains
correct: The deep places of the earth, the strength of the hills, the sea, and the dry land
explanation: God possesses universal ownership over total topography: the subterranean depths, mountain peaks, the vast oceans, and continents. Psalm 95:4-5 (KJV) - "In his hand are the deep places of the earth: the strength of the hills is his also. The sea is his, and he made it: and his hands formed the dry land."

question: What physical postures of corporate adoration are commanded in Psalm 95:6?
opt1: Stand upright, lift up holy hands, and shout with the voice of triumph
opt2: Fall flat on our faces, dance with timbrels, and leap for joy
opt3: Walk in solemn procession, blow the shofar, and bow the head
opt4: Worship, bow down, and kneel before the LORD our maker
correct: Worship, bow down, and kneel before the LORD our maker
explanation: Authentic reverence involves both inner submission and bodily posture: prostrating ('bow down') and kneeling before Yahweh the Creator. Psalm 95:6 (KJV) - "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker."

question: What intimate pastoral relationship between God and His people is confessed in Psalm 95:7?
opt1: We are the people of His pasture, and the sheep of His hand

opt3: We are the vineyard of His planting, and the branches of His root
opt4: We are the servants of His house, and the soldiers of His army
correct: We are the people of His pasture, and the sheep of His hand
explanation: Believers are depicted as a cherished flock enjoying divine pastoral sustenance ('His pasture') and personal guidance and defense ('His hand'). Psalm 95:7 (KJV) - "For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. To day if ye will hear his voice,"

question: What urgent temporal condition introduces the prophetic shift in Psalm 95:7 from joyous praise to solemn warning?
opt1: 'In the year of jubilee when the trumpet soundeth'

opt4: 'When the Son of David shall sit on His throne'
correct: 'To day if ye will hear his voice'
explanation: The divine summons demands immediate, present-tense obedience ('To day'), precluding procrastination and hardness of heart. Psalm 95:7 (KJV) - "For he is our God; and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. To day if ye will hear his voice,"

question: Which historical wilderness rebellions are recalled in Psalm 95:8 to warn Israel against hardening their hearts?
opt1: The rebellion of Korah and the golden calf at Sinai

opt3: The provocation (Meribah) and the day of temptation (Massah) in the wilderness
opt4: The murmuring at Kadesh-barnea and the fiery serpents at Hormah
correct: The provocation (Meribah) and the day of temptation (Massah) in the wilderness
explanation: Referring directly to Exodus 17:7 and Numbers 20:13, where Israel contended at Meribah ('provocation') and tested God at Massah ('temptation'). Psalm 95:8 (KJV) - "Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness:"

question: How long was God grieved with the wilderness generation who erred in their hearts, according to Psalm 95:10?
opt1: Seventy years long
opt2: Ten years long
opt3: Twenty-four years long
opt4: Forty years long
correct: Forty years long
explanation: An entire probationary generation of 40 years was spent in divine sorrow over persistent obstinacy, blindness to God's works, and refusal to know His ways. Psalm 95:10 (KJV) - "Forty years long was I grieved with this generation, and said, It is a people that do err in their heart, and they have not known my ways:"

question: What irrevocable oath did God swear in His wrath against the unbelieving wilderness generation in Psalm 95:11?
opt1: That they should not enter into His rest

correct: That they should not enter into His rest
explanation: Because of persistent unbelief, God barred that rebellious generation from entering Canaan, the physical type of His spiritual Sabbath rest. Psalm 95:11 (KJV) - "Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest."

question: Which New Testament epistle quotes Psalm 95:7-11 across two chapters to warn Christians against an evil heart of unbelief?
opt1: The Epistle to the Romans (Romans 9-11)

Psalm 95:7-11 (KJV) - "To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your heart ... Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest."

question: With what universal summons does Psalm 96:1 open, calling all creation to celebrate a fresh redemption?
opt1: Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands: serve the LORD with gladness
opt2: O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth
opt3: The LORD reigneth, let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad
opt4: Praise ye the LORD from the heavens: praise him in the heights
correct: O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth
explanation: A 'new song' celebrates newly unfolded revelations of God's redemptive glory and universal dominion, encompassing all nations across the earth. Psalm 96:1 (KJV) - "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth."

question: What global missionary mandate is proclaimed in Psalm 96:3?
opt1: Publish the law in the gates of the nations, and His statutes in distant lands
opt2: Send forth missionaries to the isles, and preach repentance to the kings
opt3: Declare his glory among the heathen, his wonders among all people

question: How does Psalm 96:5 expose the fundamental difference between pagan gods and the LORD?
opt1: The gods of the heathen have mouths but speak not: but the LORD speaketh in thunders
opt2: The idols of the Gentiles are gold and silver: but the LORD is an consuming fire
opt3: Pagan deities are the work of men's hands: but the LORD existed before all worlds
opt4: For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens
correct: For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens
explanation: Pagan gods are exposed as worthless nonentities ('elilim' - non-gods, idols), contrasted with Yahweh whose cosmic power created the vast starry heavens. Psalm 96:5 (KJV) - "For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens."

question: What divine qualities attend God's presence and reside in His holy sanctuary according to Psalm 96:6?
opt1: Honour and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary
opt2: Justice and judgment are His foundation: mercy and truth go before His face
opt3: Righteousness and peace kiss each other: salvation and light shine in His courts
opt4: Wisdom and understanding are in His mouth: glory and terror surround His ark
correct: Honour and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary
explanation: God's heavenly royal court is attended by honor and majesty, while His earthly sanctuary is crowned with divine strength and radiant holiness. Psalm 96:6 (KJV) - "Honour and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary."

question: What three actions are commanded of all the families ('kindreds') of the earth in Psalm 96:7-8?
opt1: Kneel before the high priest, burn frankincense, and swear fealty to Solomon
opt2: Give unto the LORD glory and strength, give the glory due unto His name, and bring an offering into His courts

correct: Give unto the LORD glory and strength, give the glory due unto His name, and bring an offering into His courts
explanation: All families of humanity are summoned to ascribe intrinsic majesty to Yahweh, bring freewill tribute offerings, and enter His temple courts. Psalm 96:7-8 (KJV) - "Give unto the LORD, O ye kindreds of the people, give unto the LORD glory and strength. Give unto the LORD the glory due unto his name: bring an offering, and come into his courts."

question: In what manner and attire are all the inhabitants of the earth summoned to worship the LORD in Psalm 96:9?
opt1: Worship the LORD in white linen garments: rejoice with trembling, all ye kings

correct: Worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth
explanation: 'The beauty of holiness' reflects priestly garments of spiritual sanctity, calling all nations to holy awe and reverence before God. Psalm 96:9 (KJV) - "O worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth."

question: What imperial proclamation are believers commanded to announce among the heathen in Psalm 96:10?
opt1: Proclaim to the gentiles that Jerusalem is exalted: the temple of Solomon shall stand forever

explanation: The global gospel of the Old Testament is the enthronement of Yahweh, securing planetary stability and righteous global justice. Psalm 96:10 (KJV) - "Say among the heathen that the LORD reigneth: the world also shall be established that it shall not be moved: he shall judge the people righteously."

question: Which elements of the natural cosmos are summoned to break forth into joyful celebration in Psalm 96:11-12?
opt1: The heavens, the earth, the sea with its fulness, the field with all therein, and all the trees of the wood

opt4: The rain clouds, the blooming lilies, the vineyards of En-gedi, and the cattle on a thousand hills
correct: The heavens, the earth, the sea with its fulness, the field with all therein, and all the trees of the wood
explanation: Inanimate and animate creation joins a magnificent cosmic symphony: sky, continents, oceans, cultivated fields, and wild forest trees rejoices together. Psalm 96:11-12 (KJV) - "Let the heavens rejoice, and let the earth be glad; let the sea roar, and the fulness thereof. Let the field be joyful, and all that is therein: then shall all the trees of the wood rejoice"

question: What joyful future event provokes this grand cosmic celebration at the conclusion of Psalm 96:13?

Psalm 96:13 (KJV) - "Before the LORD: for he cometh, for he cometh to judge the earth: he shall judge the world with righteousness, and the people with his truth."

question: In which historical book of the Old Testament is Psalm 96 almost verbatim recorded as part of David's festival psalm when bringing the Ark to Zion?

question: With what universal proclamation does Psalm 97:1 open, summoning both continents and distant maritime territories to rejoice?
opt1: The LORD is King for ever and ever; let the heathen tremble; let the mountains skip like rams

question: What two moral attributes are declared to be the unshakeable foundation ('habitation') of God's throne in Psalm 97:2?

explanation: Though God's transcendent presence is veiled in 'clouds and darkness', the immutable moral pillars supporting His cosmic throne are righteousness and judgment. Psalm 97:2 (KJV) - "Clouds and darkness are round about him: righteousness and judgment are the habitation of his throne."

question: How does the physical earth react when the Lord's presence and lightnings are revealed in Psalm 97:4-5?
opt1: The earth saw, and trembled; the hills melted like wax at the presence of the LORD

Psalm 97:4-5 (KJV) - "His lightnings enlightened the world: the earth saw, and trembled. The hills melted like wax at the presence of the LORD, at the presence of the Lord of the whole earth."

question: What fate is pronounced upon idolaters, and what command is issued to all celestial powers ('gods') in Psalm 97:7?

explanation: Idolaters are brought to utter confusion, while all celestial beings and subordinate powers are commanded to prostrate in worship before Yahweh (applied to Christ in Hebrews 1:6). Psalm 97:7 (KJV) - "Confounded be all they that serve graven images, that boast themselves of idols: worship him, all ye gods."

question: Why did Zion hear and rejoice, and the daughters of Judah become glad according to Psalm 97:8?

question: What ethical imperative is commanded to all who love the LORD in Psalm 97:10?

question: What divine agricultural metaphor in Psalm 97:11 describes the future joy prepared for the faithful?
opt1: Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart

question: At what specific divine attribute are the righteous summoned to give thanks in Psalm 97:12?

question: Which New Testament passage quotes the Septuagint rendering of Psalm 97:7 ('worship him, all ye gods') and applies it to angels worshipping Jesus Christ?
opt1: Colossians 1:16

question: What two protective promises does God guarantee to His saints in Psalm 97:10?
opt1: He granteth them long life, and maketh their enemies their footstool

question: By what divine instruments of power has the LORD achieved victory in Psalm 98:1?
opt1: His flaming sword, and his chariot of fire

opt3: His outstretched rod, and the breath of his nostrils

Psalm 98:1 (KJV) - "O sing unto the LORD a new song; for he hath done marvellous things: his right hand, and his holy arm, hath gotten him the victory."

question: Before whom has the LORD openly demonstrated His salvation and righteousness according to Psalm 98:2?
opt1: In the sight of the heathen

question: Which two covenant attributes has God remembered toward the house of Israel in Psalm 98:3?
opt1: His power and his holiness

explanation: Yahweh's steadfast covenant love (chesed) and unwavering faithfulness (emet) toward Israel culminate in universal salvation visible to the ends of the earth. question: Which musical instruments are specifically summoned in Psalm 98:5-6 to praise the LORD, the King?

question: What striking anthropomorphic action are the rivers ('floods') commanded to perform in Psalm 98:8?

question: With which two divine standards will the Lord judge the world and the peoples when He comes in Psalm 98:9?

question: Which famous Christian hymn, written by Isaac Watts in 1719, is a direct Christological paraphrase of Psalm 98?

question: What global geographic extent is declared to have witnessed God's redemptive work in Psalm 98:3?

question: What royal designation is given to the LORD in Psalm 98:6 before whom all musical praise is offered?

question: Between what celestial beings is the LORD described as enthroned in Psalm 99:1?

question: What solemn threefold refrain structures Psalm 99 (verses 3, 5, and 9), echoing the angelic Trisagion of Isaiah 6:3?

opt3: 'The LORD of hosts is with us' repeated three times
opt4: 'Blessed be the LORD out of Zion' repeated three times

explanation: The psalm is structured into three poetic strophes, each concluding with an emphatic affirmation of God's holiness (verses 3, 5, and 9). Psalm 99:3, 5, 9 (KJV) - "Let them praise thy great and terrible name; for it is holy ... worship at his footstool; for he is holy ... Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy hill; for the LORD our God is holy."

question: What moral quality does the King's strength love and establish in Jacob according to Psalm 99:4?
opt1: The King's sceptre loveth mercy; thou dost establish peace

opt4: The King's glory loveth sacrifice; thou dost establish the temple

question: Where are God's people commanded to worship in Psalm 99:5?

correct: At his footstool

question: Which three preeminent historical intercessors of Israel are specifically commemorated in Psalm 99:6?
opt1: Moses and Aaron among His priests, and Samuel among them that call upon His name

Psalm 99:6 (KJV) - "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among them that call upon his name; they called upon the LORD, and he answered them."

question: Through what miraculous physical manifestation did God speak to Moses and Aaron in Psalm 99:7?

question: What striking theological paradox regarding God's character toward Israel is articulated in Psalm 99:8?
opt1: Thou wast a God that smotest them, though thou rememberedst David's oath

Psalm 99:8 (KJV) - "Thou answeredst them, O LORD our God: thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of their inventions."

question: Where are believers commanded to worship in the culminating doxology of Psalm 99:9?
opt1: In the heavens above

question: What effect should the announcement of Yahweh's reign produce upon the nations and the earth according to Psalm 99:1?

question: Why is Samuel specifically grouped alongside Moses and Aaron as an intercessor in Psalm 99:6?

explanation: Samuel's legacy was defined by powerful intercession: 'God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you' (1 Samuel 12:23). Psalm 99:6 (KJV) - "Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among them that call upon his name; they called upon the LORD, and he answered them."

question: What is the unique Hebrew title given to Psalm 100 in its superscription?

question: With what universal invitation to sacred joy and worship does Psalm 100:1-2 open?
opt1: Bow down before the sanctuary, all ye tribes: offer sacrifices with weeping and fasting

explanation: True biblical service is characterized by joyful enthusiasm and celebration, inviting all nations into God's presence with jubilant singing. Psalm 100:1-2 (KJV) - "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands. Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing."

question: What fundamental theological reality regarding human origins and divine ownership is confessed in Psalm 100:3?
opt1: We have formed ourselves by wisdom; we are the kings of creation and masters of our fate
opt2: We were born of dust and return to ashes; we are shadows passing through a weary land

opt4: It is He that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture

explanation: Radically denying human autonomy or self-creation, the text establishes that God is our Creator, Owner, and Shepherd, while we are His dependent flock. Psalm 100:3 (KJV) - "Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture."

question: What two progressive architectural entries of the temple are specified in Psalm 100:4, and with what attitudes must worshippers enter them?
opt1: Enter into His gates with thanksgiving, and into His courts with praise

question: What threefold eternal character of God forms the supreme rationale for thanksgiving in Psalm 100:5?
opt1: The LORD is holy; his throne is exalted; and his dominion is over all flesh

explanation: The ultimate grounds of adoration rest upon God's essential benevolence ('good'), unending covenant love ('mercy/chesed'), and perpetual faithfulness ('truth/emunah'). Psalm 100:5 (KJV) - "For the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth endureth to all generations."

question: What vital truth does the phrase 'not we ourselves' in Psalm 100:3 communicate against human pride?

Psalm 100:3 (KJV) - "Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture."

question: What two concluding imperatives are addressed to worshippers in Psalm 100:4?
opt1: Be thankful unto him, and bless his name

question: How far into time does God's truth (emunah) extend according to Psalm 100:5?

question: Who is invited to participate in this grand celebration of worship in Psalm 100:1?
opt1: Only the consecrated priests of the line of Ithamar

question: What two overarching divine principles form the theme of David's song in Psalm 101:1?

question: Where does David vow to walk with a 'perfect heart' in Psalm 101:2?

explanation: True spiritual integrity is tested not on public display, but in private domestic life behind closed doors ('within my house'). Psalm 101:2 (KJV) - "I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart."

question: What solemn resolve does David make regarding his visual intake and entertainment in Psalm 101:3?
opt1: I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes

explanation: David establishes an eye-covenant, refusing to gaze upon or entertain any base, worthless, or immoral spectacle ('thing of Belial'). Psalm 101:3 (KJV) - "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me."

question: What two character flaws does David refuse to tolerate in Psalm 101:5?
opt1: Him that hath slow hands and a fearful spirit

opt4: Him that hath lean cattle and an impoverished house

explanation: Haughty arrogance ('high look') and internal self-exaltation ('proud heart') are utterly intolerable in the court of a godly monarch. Psalm 101:5 (KJV) - "Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer."

question: What severe consequence does David declare for anyone who covertly slanders his neighbor in Psalm 101:5?
opt1: Him will I fine with thirty shekels of silver

opt3: Him will I cut off
opt4: Him will I rebuke before the assembly of the congregation
correct: Him will I cut off
explanation: Secret character assassination and whispering slander are treated with maximum royal severity: immediate banishment and cutting off. Psalm 101:5 (KJV) - "Whoso privily slandereth his neighbour, him will I cut off: him that hath an high look and a proud heart will not I suffer."

question: Whom does David seek out to dwell in his palace and serve in his administration in Psalm 101:6?
opt1: The mighty men of valor who slew thousands of Philistines

Psalm 101:6 (KJV) - "Mine eyes shall be upon the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me: he that walketh in a perfect way, he shall serve me."

question: Which two categories of corrupt individuals are strictly forbidden from dwelling in David's house or remaining in his sight in Psalm 101:7?

opt4: He that is weak in battle, and he that hath no lineage

question: When and why did David resolve to administer justice against the wicked according to Psalm 101:8?
opt1: At the feast of tabernacles, that Jerusalem might be filled with righteous sacrifices

opt3: In the evening twilight, that the blood of the guilty might cleanse the land
opt4: Once every seven years, that debts might be canceled and slaves set free
correct: I will early destroy all the wicked of the land, that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the LORD
explanation: In ancient Israel, court was convened early each morning; David resolved each dawn to purge Jerusalem of crime and maintain sanctuary purity. Psalm 101:8 (KJV) - "I will early destroy all the wicked of the land; that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the LORD."

question: What historical moniker is frequently applied to Psalm 101 by biblical commentators due to its practical guidance for rulers and leaders?

Psalm 101:1-8 (KJV) - "I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way ... I will walk within my house with a perfect heart."

question: What tender, expectant question does David cry out in Psalm 101:2, expressing his longing for divine fellowship and guidance?

question: What unique descriptive superscription belongs to Psalm 102, identifying the author not by name but by spiritual condition?

question: Which three solitary birds are invoked in Psalm 102:6-7 to depict the psalmist's profound isolation and desolation?

question: What somatic manifestations of acute anguish and physical wasting does the afflicted author describe in Psalm 102:3-5?

opt4: Strength dried up like a potsherd, garments rotting like moth-eaten wool, and teeth broken with gravel

question: What sorrowful diet does the afflicted sufferer consume in Psalm 102:9?

question: Why does the psalmist possess absolute confidence in Psalm 102:13 that God will arise and restore devastated Zion?

question: What tender affection do God's exiled servants display toward the ruins of Jerusalem in Psalm 102:14?

question: For whom is this divine restoration of Zion recorded according to Psalm 102:18?
opt1: For the scribes of Judah to preserve in the royal chronicles of David

question: What two compassionate purposes prompted the LORD to look down from the height of His sanctuary in Psalm 102:19-20?

question: How does Psalm 102:25-27 contrast the temporary, wearing cosmos with the eternal immutability of God?

question: What internal spiritual self-charge opens David's great psalm of thanksgiving in Psalm 103:1-2?

explanation: David marshals all his internal faculties ('all that is within me') to praise Yahweh, commanding himself never to suffer spiritual amnesia regarding God's gracious benefits. question: Which five personal benefits of redemption are enumerated in Psalm 103:3-5?
opt1: Giving victory over enemies, multiplying silver and gold, establishing an earthly house, preserving health, and giving long life
